title: Representation
oneLine: Preferred way of representing information and experience.
frontSummary: Preferred way of representing information and experience.
definition: Representation describes how people take in external sensory information and reproduce it internally as images, sounds, body sensations, or words.
languageCues: Visual: see, view, looks right, picture
behaviouralSigns: Auditory: attends to tone and sound
blindSpots: May miss other forms of information
May assume others process the same way
coachingPrompts: Do you need to see it, hear it, feel it, or put it into words?
How are you representing this internally?

example: A visual client may prefer a diagram; a language-oriented client may prefer written steps.

title: Epistemological
oneLine: Preferred way of gathering information: through sensory facts or inner intuition.
frontSummary: Preferred way of gathering information: through sensory facts or inner intuition.
definition: Epistemological sorting describes whether a person gathers information primarily through observable sensory data or through inner knowing, meaning, possibility, and intuition.
languageCues: Intuitor: possibility, meaning, pattern, gut feeling
behaviouralSigns: Sensor: checks what can be seen, heard, or measured
Intuitor: reads between the lines and infers meaning
blindSpots: Sensor: may miss meaning or implication
coachingPrompts: What do you notice directly?
What do you intuit this means?
visualScene: A person comparing a clipboard of facts with a glowing inner compass.
example: A sensor may want proof; an intuitor may sense what the pattern is pointing toward.

title: Scale / Scope

What does this connect to?

title: Self-Experience
oneLine: What aspect of self a person identifies with most strongly.
frontSummary: What aspect of self a person identifies with most strongly.
definition: Self-Experience describes how a person defines and experiences self through mind, emotion, will, body, role, spirit, or disidentification from all of these.

behaviouralSigns: Identity language reveals the dominant self-experience

Which part of you feels most real?

title: Self-Instruction
oneLine: How a person responds to being told, instructed, or directed.
frontSummary: How a person responds to being told, instructed, or directed.
definition: Self-Instruction describes whether a person naturally complies with instruction, balances instruction with choice, or resists being told what to do.
languageCues: Strong-willed: don’t tell me, I resist
coachingPrompts: How do you respond to instructions?
What wording preserves choice?

title: Self-Confidence
oneLine: Sense of competence in ability, skill, and capacity.
frontSummary: Sense of competence in ability, skill, and capacity.
definition: Self-Confidence describes a person’s felt competence in doing, performing, or applying a skill. It is about capacity, not inherent worth.
coachingPrompts: Where do you feel competent?
What evidence of ability can you count?
visualScene: A person hesitating before a task beside another standing confidently with tools.

title: Self-Esteem
oneLine: Whether self-worth is treated as earned or inherent.
frontSummary: Whether self-worth is treated as earned or inherent.
definition: Self-Esteem describes how a person relates to their worth as a human being. Conditional self-esteem links value to performance; unconditional self-esteem recognises inherent worth.
languageCues: Conditional: prove myself, only if, earn it
Unconditional: I have worth, I matter
blindSpots: Unconditional: can be misunderstood as no accountability
coachingPrompts: Is your worth conditional here?
What changes if worth is inherent?
visualScene: A person looking in a mirror with trophies on one side and calm acceptance on the other.
example: A person can improve performance without making mistakes mean they are worthless.

title: Self-Integrity
oneLine: Congruence between ideal self, values, and lived behaviour.
frontSummary: Congruence between ideal self, values, and lived behaviour.
definition: Self-Integrity describes whether a person feels internally conflicted and incongruent or aligned and integrated with their values and ideal self.
behaviouralSigns: Conflicted: says one thing and lives another
blindSpots: Integrated: can become rigidity if idealised
coachingPrompts: Where are you out of alignment?

example: Integrity increases when behaviour matches values.

title: Self-Monitoring

frontSummary: Ability to notice internal thoughts, emotions, needs, and impulses.

title: Time Experience
oneLine: How time is internally represented and experienced.
frontSummary: How time is internally represented and experienced.
definition: Time Experience describes whether a person is inside time, observing time from a meta position, or experiencing time in more random/sequential patterns.

title: Values
oneLine: What a person treats as important, meaningful, and significant.
frontSummary: What a person treats as important, meaningful, and significant.
